source.title: Is Refusal Direction Universal across Low-Resourced Languages?

page_placements.theme: Multilingual and prompt-framing transfer: harm separation and direction-based interventions weaken in non-English and low-resource languages

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: Applies difference-in-means refusal directions and tests ablation and addition effects on refusal-related behavior in new language settings, using the same kind of intervention and behavioral measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports cross-language ablation and addition outcomes, plus normalized ablation effects. Figure-only values without a textual result, including some Yoruba results, are not extracted. Results cited from Arditi et al. and Wang et al. are not rows.
record.test_reason: Applies the difference-in-means refusal direction (following Wang et al. 2025) to Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. It reports ablation and addition effects on WildGuard compliance for three new low-resource languages. This tests V1 in a new setting and tests V6 cross-language transfer. The measure is WildGuard compliance, not the original refusal-substring and safety scoring, so T3 fits better than T1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that universality is graded. English and Belarusian directions transfer to all tested targets, and English's normalized effect on Bashkir and Tajik is substantial despite ceiling effects. Bashkir and Tajik directions fail to modulate refusal on any target, including themselves, once baselines are accounted for. Geometric alignment and behavioral transfer are partially dissociated, with Bashkir and Tajik signals aligning with English at other layers. Users of strongly misaligned low-resource languages get weaker safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means refusal-direction pipeline and ablation/addition behavioral tests, extended to multilingual transfer on one model. The paper describes following Wang et al. (2025); it does not establish that every intervention detail, including layer and position scope, matches the original Arditi et al. procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer depends on source-language safety alignment; Belarusian-to-Bashkir transfer is weaker. Baseline ceiling effects alter interpretation of raw compliance changes. Cross-layer alignment peaks differ by source language.

fits_no_version.finding: Silhouette separation of harmful vs harmless representations at layer 30 ranks English 0.356, Belarusian 0.169, Yoruba 0.085, Tajik 0.065, Bashkir 0.046. The ranking tracks transfer effectiveness.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: How well harmful and harmless prompts are separated in a language's representations predicts how well refusal-direction interventions work in that language.

record.problems: All experiments use one model. Only a small number of added languages are tested. The authors note that machine-translation quality is uncertain and manual verification was not by native speakers of the target languages, with the lowest verification confidence for Bashkir. The study does not test harmless-request false refusals or general capability retention. Confidence intervals are bootstrap resamples of existing judgments and representations, without rerunning model inference.
record.rows_left_out: Figure-only results without corresponding textual values or explicit descriptions, including some Yoruba and addition results in Figures 2 and 4, were not extracted. Figure 8 details without a textual numerical or qualitative result were not separately recorded.

untested.parts: Inducing refusal on harmless prompts by addition. Retention of general capabilities after ablation. Other model families. Addition is tested only for the English direction.
Transfer across model variants or from base to instruct models. Other models than Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Yoruba results are figure-only.

missing.what: Qualitative geometric result: refusal directions are parallel to English only for Belarusian and diverge for Bashkir, Tajik and Yoruba (PCA). This contrasts with Wang et al.'s parallelism across all languages.
Yoruba ablation and addition results with the English direction, used as a reference point.
Normalized effect of the Bashkir direction on English, stated in the text as Δ = 0.01.

record.verdict_notes: Single model, Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. It replicates Wang et al. (2025), not Arditi et al. directly, and is not an original source. R21–R25 recompute R07, R11, R16, R12 and R15 as normalized Δ, so they duplicate those rows. Baselines are no-intervention compliance from Table 2 and have no CI; the CIs are bootstrap over existing judgments only. The text has internal slips: it says the ceiling effect is revisited 'in Section 5.2' (it is 5.3), and it cites 'Appendix 8' for Figure 8. Below-baseline self-ablation values are labelled reversed by the numbers, but the authors interpret them as noise or no effect.

versions.untested_parts: Tests refusal-related compliance after direction ablation and harmful-request compliance after adding the English direction. Does not test false refusal on harmless requests, general capability retention, or whether projection at every layer and position is required.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration experiment.
Does not test whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, conic, or multi-direction account.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Tests cross-language transfer on Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct. Does not test transfer across model variants, from base to instruct models, or across the full set of languages.
Does not manipulate or compare refusal-training procedures or stages.

relation.reason: Its own difference-in-means ablation and addition results bear on V1 and V6.

tranche.reason: The study's stated aim and result is that the cross-language universality version (V6) needs restating. Transfer is graded and fails from strongly misaligned sources; the authors say the results refine universality. T5 is listed ahead of T3. T3 would also fit the design. It is not T1, because the measure is WildGuard compliance, not the original's substring and Llama Guard 2 scores.

source_check.notes: One model (Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct), machine-translated prompts, no random-direction control or capability check. Baselines are Table 2 percents, post-ablation values Table 4 fractions; Yoruba results are figure-only. Rows R03-R05, R07-R10, R13, R15 are V1,V6 but R12, R14, R21, R24, R25 are V6 only. Author is at MaiNLP, LMU Munich, as are Wang et al. 2025's Plank and Schütze (affiliation outside the text), so it may not be independent of 2505.17306.

statements.problem: Minor: the Bashkir self-ablation figure is a fall below baseline (delta -1.30), so refusal rises. The statement shows the numbers but does not say this.
Minor: '4.9%->0.998 with the English direction' is English direction on English prompts. On Bashkir and Tajik prompts the English direction gives 0.977 and 0.991.

statements.correction: 2610.28897: English-direction ablation on Belarusian (class 3, baseline 24.7%) gives 0.998, on Bashkir (class 1, 87.9%) 0.977, on Tajik (class 1, 92.0%) 0.991 (Table 4; Table 1 resource classes).
statements.problem: The conditions say targets are safety-aligned or higher-resource. In this study, Bashkir and Tajik are resource class 1 and strongly misaligned. Belarusian is class 3 and partially aligned. The part specific to this study is truncated and cannot be checked.

statements.correction: be->en 0.932, be->tg 0.965, be->ba delta 0.13. Bashkir-English cos about -0.01 at layer 30 only; Bashkir alignment peaks at layers 35-40, Tajik at 20-25 (Fig 8). Self-ablation delta: ba -1.30, tg 0.00. R10/R13/R14 delta about 0.25/0.30/0.63. The authors 'refine' universality to aligned sources.
statements.problem: Overbroad for this study. Belarusian is also low-resource, yet its direction aligns with English and transfers. Near-orthogonality holds only at layer 30. The Bashkir and Tajik directions also fail on their own language. Several cited rows show partial rises, not absence. These are limits_scope, not challenges.

statements.correction: 2610.28897 addition: Bashkir 0.88->0.41, Tajik 0.92->0.43 (partial), Belarusian 0.24->0.01. English ablation: Bashkir delta about 0.81 (0.977), Tajik delta about 0.89 (0.991).
statements.problem: Filed under challenges, but in this study English-direction addition roughly halves Bashkir and Tajik compliance. That is partial (the record's own V6 label is limits_scope), not nil or negative. English ablation transfers almost fully to these targets, and addition works fully on low-resource Belarusian.
Minor: the paper ties the failure to alignment tier, not resource level (Belarusian is low-resource and transfers). The Bashkir direction also fails on Bashkir itself (delta -1.30).

Correct for this study: English-direction transfer is reproduced by ablation, and by addition (full for Belarusian, partial for Bashkir and Tajik), on one model. See notes on whether it is independent of arXiv:2505.17306.

reader_labels.reason: The normalized effect is positive but weak (∆ = 0.13), and the authors identify it as markedly weaker than other transfer results (R07, R21).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Bashkir and Tajik source directions, after accounting for target-language baseline compliance
reader_labels.reason: The authors report near-zero or negative normalized effects for these sources, including on themselves and each other; the explicit results include negative Bashkir effects and zero Tajik self-effect (R11–R16, R22–R25).
